To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

perceived hedonic and perceived utilitarian benefits positively predict users’ self-disclosure, whereas perceived privacy risks and perceived privacy benefits predict users’ selfdisclosure negatively.
the privacy calculus and benefit structures influence self-disclosure on wearables, and that these factors are different for prospective users, current users, and former users.

(1) prospective users are more likely to disclose personal information on wearable devices if the benefits outweigh the privacy risks; (2) current users are more likely disclose personal information on their wearable devices if they perceive more hedonic benefits; (3) current users are less likely disclose personal information if they perceive more utilitarian benefits; (4) former users are more likely cease continued use of wearable devices when they perceive more utiliarian benefits.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the factors that affect users’ decisions to disclose personal information on wearable devices, and the factors that affect their decision to cease continued use of wearable devices.
understanding users’ decision-making processes regarding self-disclosure of wearable device data.
understanding how and why users decide to self-disclose using wearable devices.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

this study contributes to the literature by providing an integrated conceptual model that examines the roles of benefit structure, privacy calculus, and self-disclosure among different types of wearable device users.
privacy calculus and benefit structures influence users’ self-disclosure on their wearable devices.
the results of the study indicate that the privacy calculus model can be used to explain self-disclosure behavior of prospective, current, as well as former users of wearable technology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
privacy calculus and benefit perceptions are crucial factors that influence users’ self-disclosure on the wearable devices.
users’ perceived benefits and privacy calculus are the two key antecedents for their decision to disclose or not to disclose on wearable devices.
the privacy calculus is more salient for prospective and current users, while perceived benefits are more important for former users.
The main takeaway from our work is that
privacy calculus plays a critical role in users’ decision-making regarding self-disclosure on these devices.
privacy concerns and perceived benefit are important factors that affect self-disclosure.
users’ self-disclosure behavior is not a simple binary choice.
